## What changed

**The temporary apt configuration carried a Cyrillic comment.** That file is
read by apt, not by a person, and every byte outside ASCII in it is a bet that
someone else's parser — on a version we cannot test — behaves exactly like the
one on the developer's machine. The stake is the only setting that matters
there: without the proxy, on a closed network, not a single package downloads.
The comment is ASCII now, and a test refuses any byte above 126 in that file.

This surfaced while chasing a real failure where `apt-get -c <our file> update`
returned exit 100 on the repository while the identical settings passed as
`-o` returned 0, on the same machine, seconds apart. On apt 2.8 the `-c` form
is provably equivalent: it applies the proxy (verified by a SOCKS server
logging the CONNECT) and does not suppress `apt.conf.d`. Whether the comment is
what apt 2.0 stumbles on is still unproven — but a config file for another
program is no place to find out.

Nothing else about the mechanism changed: the settings still go to a temporary
file passed with `-c` rather than into `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/`, so `kill -9`
leaves the system unconfigured, and the proxy password never appears in
`ps aux`.
